BASIC BUS SYSTEM PROTOCOL
DISCUSSION
Basic Bus System Protocol defines terminology used in conjunction with bus system protocol, and describes the operational characteristics of the basic bus system and tri-state devices.
Since a microprocessor (CPU) contains all the functional sections of a computer, it is easy to discuss bus organization by analyzing the CPU operation.
The unidirectional control bus originates in the control section. It supplies inputs to the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), the on-chip memory sections and to external units.
The unidirectional address bus also originates in the control section. The address routing is to both on-chip memory and external units.
All the functional sections of a CPU are connected to the data bus. This allows bi-directional data flow to the ALU, memory and external units.
CPU input/output can be shown as a single functional block with all buses supplying either control, address, or data information.
Unidirectional buses interface with the system bus via bus transmitters. These transmitters isolate the CPU from the external sources.

The size of the address bus is determined by the memory capacity of the total system. For example, a 64K memory would require 16 separate address lines.
The control bus is unidirectional. It carries the synchronization and enable signals necessary to allow flow of information.
The control bus also carries information describing what operation is to be performed, and which units are to respond. Signals include timing, memory read/write, and I/O read/write.
Control, data, and address buses extend into each of the separate system components enabling all components to gain access to the bus signals.
System components utilizing buses avoid massive interference by the application of gates, and precise timing. The CPU/controller contains the clock for precise timing of the system.
Each component is connected to each bus wire through a gating network which consists of hundreds of AND gates.

One input of each gate connects to a specific bus line, the second to a timing source, and the third to the control section. The information on the bus line is passed only when its AND gate is enabled.
Memory is divided into three types; read-only memory (ROM), random-access memory (RAM), and single word locations (registers).
ROM contains the necessary steps required to sequence the CPU through initialization. ROM is permanent memory and does not change or erase when power is removed.
The term RAM generally indicates read/write random access memory. All RAM may be manipulated under program control. The data in this memory is lost when power is removed.
RAM and ROM are housed in arrays of storage cells. These may be accessed by the CPU in groups of eight cells (8-bit bytes) called addresses.
Random access to RAM and ROM is accomplished by placing the binary equivalent of the address on the address bus. When the address appears on the address bus, that location in memory is accessed.
The CPU/controller determines whether to decode (READ) or store (WRITE) the information at the accessed location.

The final type of memory we'll cover is single word memory locations. Single word memory locations (registers) inside the microprocessor are provided for information manipulation. Registers provide temporary storage of information.
DISCUSSION
The basic bus system block diagram is comprised of four parts: Microprocessor (CPU/controller), System Memory, and System Input/Output.
A bus line is a conductor or conductive solder path that connects multiple components, functions or systems.
Multiple components sharing a bus line must be controlled to enable an orderly transfer of data.
Initially, computers required two buses. These were unidirectional and commands could only move in one direction. Two buses take up more space and increase cost.
For convenience, we will use a microcomputer system block diagram as an example.
The system bus is comprised of three different buses; Data, Address, and Control.

The data bus transmits and receives bytes of data and instructions. The word size (8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit, etc.) determines the number of conductors required. An 8-bit data bus requires 8 parallel lines.
The data bus is bi-directional and carries information to and from system components. Direction of data flow is determined by the control signals generated in the microprocessor.
The CPU selects a path on the address bus using control signals. The information requested is transmitted to or from the CPU on the data bus.
The address data instructions are critical in determining which component receives the intelligence data. Misdirected data could lock up a system, making it's circuitry useless.
Tri-state devices allow the use of bi-directional bus systems. Data can be transferred in an out of a microprocessor on one bus. Systems are easily expanded by using more than one bus.
In order to take advantage of the billions of bits of usable data, new systems must operate error free at high speeds and greater distances.
